newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa successor vote soon - church official.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa successor vote soon - church official.

text.p: A delayed election to find a successor to Mother Teresa to lead her Missionaries of Charity Roman Catholic order may be held any day now, a senior church official said on Tuesday.
The election to find a successor to the ailing 86-year-old charismatic nun was originally scheduled for September 8 last year but has been postponed twice due to her poor health.
"It can happen any day now but we cannot say when. The deliberations are still going on," Father Antony Rodrigues, secretary to the Archbishop of Calcutta, told Reuters.
It was rescheduled for February 2 this year but postponed again after the electoral college of the Missionaries of Charity decided to hold a month of discussions.
Sources close to the order said the election process should be completed by March 15 because overseas delegates were booked on flights out of India on March 16.
A Missionaries of Charity spokeswoman, however, said she could not confirm or deny the delegates' itineraries.
The religious leader's health has improved and she was in good spirits, the spokeswoman said. "She (Mother Teresa) is much better and doing well."
But only a handful of the order's foreign volunteers were allowed to meet her at her current residence in Mother House, the order's Calcutta headquarters, the spokeswoman said.
The 1979 Nobel Peace laureate, affectionately known as "Mother", had wanted to step down in 1990, a year after she was fitted with a pacemaker, but was persuaded to stay on.
She has led the order from the start, shaping the mission's work with her strong personality. But she now wants to retire because of heart, kidney and lung problems.
Mother Teresa founded the order in 1949. It now guides the lives of some 4,500 nuns working to help the poor in about 80 countries.

Known by many as the "Saint of the Gutters" for her work with the poor and the destitute, Mother Teresa spent three weeks in hospital last August and September for heart trouble, malaria and pneumonia.
Two weeks later, she fell off a chair and hit her head.
She was admitted to hospital again in November to unblock two coronary arteries for the third such operation in five years.

Mother Teresa returned home shortly before Christmas after a long period of recovery delayed by bronchitis and a irregular heartbeat. Her doctors have cautioned she might never be as active as before.
The chapel inside the Mother House, which is normally open to visitors, has been closed since January 16 when a retreat to discuss Mother Teresa's successor began.
The nuns of the religious order hold their prayer meetings in the chapel. The chapel is now only open to the members of the General Chapter, the electoral college.
The chapel will be reopened to the public again in mid-March, the spokeswoman said.
"This time there are 132 members in the General Chapter and they have come from all over the world," a senior church official said.
The election process involves the 132 members of the order's electoral order, or the General Chapter.
